title: As GLP-1 Drugs Get Cheaper in India, Doctors Warn of Hidden Nutritional Risks
excerpt: With semaglutide patents expiring and generic competition set to slash prices, Indian physicians are urging structured nutritional and exercise support to prevent muscle loss and nutrient deficiencies in patients on weight-loss medications.
body:
• India's semaglutide patent expiration in March 2026 will lead to a significant drop in GLP-1 drug prices, with generics projected to cost ₹3,000–5,000 per month.
  • Doctors warn that GLP-1 drugs can cause muscle loss and require structured nutritional support to mitigate risks.
  • Unsupervised use of GLP-1 drugs by non-medical professionals is a concern among healthcare providers.
  • Experts recommend increased protein intake and resistance training for patients undergoing GLP-1 therapy.
Key Takeaways
  • India's semaglutide patent expired in March 2026, enabling generics to reduce costs significantly.
  • GLP-1 drugs can lead to muscle loss, necessitating structured nutritional support for users.
  • Doctors warn against unsupervised use of GLP-1 drugs by non-medical professionals.
  • Experts recommend higher protein intake and resistance training for patients on GLP-1 therapy.

India is on the cusp of a GLP-1 revolution. With the patent on semaglutide — the active molecule behind Novo Nordisk's blockbuster drugs Ozempic and Wegovy — expiring in the country in March 2026, major Indian pharmaceutical firms including Cipla, Sun Pharma, Dr Reddy's, Biocon, and Zydus Lifesciences are racing to market generic versions. Analysts at Jefferies predict the domestic semaglutide market could eventually reach $1 billion.

But as prices fall and access expands, Indian doctors are raising an alarm that has echoed through the global medical community: without proper nutritional and exercise support, the drugs' appetite-suppressing effects can strip patients of muscle, bone density, and essential micronutrients.

The Promise and the Price Tag

India's anti-obesity drug sector has grown from roughly $16 million in 2021 to close to $100 million, according to research firm Pharmarack. Monthly treatment with branded Ozempic costs ₹8,800–11,000, while Wegovy runs ₹10,000–16,000 — prohibitive for most Indians. Generic competition could push costs down to ₹3,000–5,000 per month, potentially opening access for millions in a country with more than 77 million people living with type 2 diabetes.

Mumbai-based bariatric surgeon Muffazal Lakdawala calls the drugs a potential game-changer but adds a caveat. "The quality of the drugs being made here must be very tightly regulated," he told The Business Standard. "We do not want side effects arising from poor-quality medicines and giving the molecule itself a bad name."

The Muscle Loss Problem

GLP-1 receptor agonists work by mimicking a gut hormone that signals satiety, reducing caloric intake by up to 39%. While the drugs preferentially reduce fat mass — including visceral and ectopic fat — they also produce consistent reductions in lean mass. A comprehensive review published in Metabolites in May 2026 found that the most effective countermeasure combines food-first nutritional counseling, adequate protein intake, structured resistance exercise, and management of gastrointestinal side effects.

The recommended daily protein intake for patients on GLP-1 therapy is 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram of adjusted body weight — roughly double what many Indians currently consume. Clinical guidelines also call for monitoring of vitamin D, B12, iron, folate, zinc, and thiamine, nutrients that can become depleted when appetite suppression reduces overall food intake.

"If a senior loses weight but also loses significant muscle mass, is the treatment really a success?"

— Alissa Chen, Yale School of Medicine

A University of California, San Francisco study published in Radiology in July 2026 added urgency to the concern. Researchers found that people whose weight repeatedly fluctuated — a pattern common among those who start and stop GLP-1 drugs — lost nearly four times as much thigh muscle over four years as those with stable weight.

Misuse Concerns as Access Widens

Nutritional Needs for GLP-1 Users
›Recommended protein intake: 1.2–1.6 g/kg body weight
›Monitor for deficiencies in vitamin D, B12, iron, and zinc
›Structured resistance training is essential
›Daily protein intake should be prioritized at every meal

Indian physicians report a troubling pattern emerging even before generics flood the market. Gym trainers, beauty clinics, and dieticians without prescribing authority are recommending high doses. Online pharmacies dispense the drugs after cursory consultations. Beauticians advertise rapid slimming packages timed to weddings and social events.

"People come asking to lose 10 kg in three months," says Mumbai-based diabetologist Rahul Baxi. He insists on lifestyle and dietary improvements before prescribing and starts patients on higher-protein diets with a registered dietician. "Current evidence suggests the drugs may need to be taken over the long term. But many patients arrive asking for a quick fix after seeing Instagram reels."

India's drug regulator has responded with an advisory warning pharmaceutical companies against promoting prescription weight-loss medicines directly to consumers, stressing that such drugs should only be used under medical supervision.

What Patients Should Know

International consensus guidelines published in Obesity Medicine in 2026 outline 52 evidence-based recommendations for patients on GLP-1 therapy. The core prescription is straightforward: prioritize protein at every meal (targeting 0.3–0.4 g/kg per meal with adequate leucine), add progressive resistance training at least twice weekly, and maintain regular check-ups including body composition assessments via DXA or bioelectrical impedance analysis.

Risks of Unsupervised GLP-1 Use
›Non-medical professionals prescribing GLP-1 drugs
›Patients seeking rapid weight loss without medical guidance
›Concerns over drug quality and side effects
›Regulatory warnings against direct consumer promotion

For the Indian market specifically, clinicians note that traditional vegetarian diets may require careful supplementation to hit protein targets. Dal, paneer, and curd provide a foundation, but patients may need whey or plant-based protein supplements to reach therapeutic levels while eating less overall.

As Baxi puts it: "Access calls for more responsibility and stricter regulation. I am cautiously optimistic about these drugs."
